There was one that I recall here in the Boston area, at Emmanuel Church was it? The So What – that’s where the So What recording was made.

That was a band that was put together with a number of people from New England Conservatory, but also others out in the street, the streets of Boston. It was called African Game. I like to think that that’s one of my best, because of its visits to different places and different feelings. It turned out very well. Bruce Lundvall has kept it a secret for many, many years. That secret’s going to explode soon.
That’s Bruce Lundvall of Blue Note Records?
Yeah.

It was a – I remember that it was a commission for about 25 musicians? There were two Grammy nominations that came forward, once the record actually came out itself. I think one was for best big band performance, and one was for best instrumental arrangement. It was a very fine record. The vertical form was prevalent, strong, throughout, the rhythmic aspect of it, as well as all of the orchestrations, a fantastic record.

I don’t believe much in giveaways in terms of – that happen when people perform and it’s an audience of all kinds of people that are hired as raiders. I think African Game deserved a Grammy, not just two recognitions. It deserved a Grammy, because what got the Grammy was not anywhere near what African Game is. I’m glad I’m giving you the high down and the lowdown. Okay?

I think you’re absolutely right. It’s interesting, because the ’80s kind of started off with a focus on two people in the music, and the music’s much bigger than that. But it was understandable that people were focusing on and excited about the return of Miles Davis, which at the time was a possible return. About a year later, in ’81, he did actually get back into the music game, the business of making music, the art of making music. But the other person who many people feel unfairly received a lot of attention was the young unknown trumpet player out of New Orleans, Wynton Marsalis. The politics that were and are associated with that are still going on. But you’re absolutely right. Many people, and I would be among many people when I say this, thought that The African Game should have won a Grammy, not only for the two categories it was nominated, but for one or two other categories as well. Unfortunately the music business and the business of music politics is an ugly game. There’s no question about it. You had a lot of wonderful recordings, though, in the 1980s, as I mentioned earlier. The recording that was subsequently titled The New York Big Band: Live at the Village Vanguard came out at the beginning of 1980. There was Live in an American Time Spiral, which was to me a fantastic recording. I always liked that, the tune Time Spiral. There’s Ezz-thetics for Ezzard Charles, who was someone that you knew, a great heavyweight boxer. They don’t talk too much about Ezzard Charles and Jersey Joe Walcott anymore, but they were – they had a lot to do with boxing remaining a vital sport at the time when they were both practicing their art, as well as science, of boxing. We haven’t heard that tune from you in a long time, as I think about it, Ezz-thetics, or any thematic elements that I recognize as Ezz-thetics. Have I missed something somewhere along the line?
I’m not one to go back.
That’s true.
I don’t go backwards. I don’t travel that way. I always want to grow, bigger, stronger, more interesting, and explore.
Some other recordings from the period: Electronic Sonata again, re-released this time by a person we’ve spoken of recently, Bonandrini on his Soul Note label; and a record made called Live in Tokyo.
That was done in Tokyo, live concert.
Also a concert called The London Concert, at the end of the decade, 1989.
Also not in America.
London, England.
The Barbican in London.

Both of those came in the early years in which your Living Time Orchestra, which goes back to I think the ’70s – correct me if I’m wrong – had kind of evolved or developed into what was now being called the International Living Time Orchestra. You had been invited by the Contemporary Music Network of the British Council, I believe, to do a tour with some British and American musicians?
Yes, that’s true.
Tell us about that. That’s quite an honor.

Good players, the Brits. No problems in terms of psychological moods or anything. They’re totally cooperative. Played their heads off. Still do. And a nice group of people. I have been out at times when the psychological makeup of one or two people was very unpleasant. Bandleaders know about that. I try to avoid that in my travels. And that’s what I do. I travel. Not in America, but in every other place.
Hi. I’m Bob Daughtry. Today is Wednesday, May 5th, 2004, Cinco de Mayo. I’m here with George and Alice Russell for the Smithsonian Oral History Project. Katea Stitt is engineering. This is tape 4.
George, you’re looking like you’re hanging better that I am.
That’s a high compliment, for both of us.
Alice, how are you?
Very well, Bob, thank you.
Thanks for joining us. We really do appreciate it.
My pleasure.
How did you all meet?

I was director of a community music school in St. Louis in the inner city in the mid-’70s. We had a longstanding relationship with the New England Conservatory for them to use our space to audition possible students for the Conservatory. One year the director of admissions, whose name was Bill Mahon, brought George with him to recruit for the jazz department. I found out later that George hated having to do this, wanted nothing to do with recruiting anything for the New England Conservatory, but we met and had dinner that evening and then began a kind of commuting relationship for the next year, until I moved to Boston.
That was what year?
That would have – we met in ’76. I moved to Boston in ’77.
And you all are married now.
Yes, for 27 years.
27 years. Congratulations.
Thank you.

In today’s world that’s fantastic. That really is. We’ve been – we’ve covered a lot of territory so far, George. We’re about to move into the ’90s. I know that the ’90s for all of us have been tremendously traumatic at times and very turbulent. The decade opened with the Gulf War, and it’s just been crazy ever since. The economy is up and then it’s down, and all of the stuff with the presidents. So politically, the times have been turbulent. Economically, they’ve been a roller coaster.

Socially, they’ve been the pastiche and the mish-mash of crazy things that they’ve always been, or it seems like in my lifetime. Musically, it’s been both feast and famine. There have been some interesting and wonderful points, like a concert that you did for the New England Conservatory of Music in 1992, I believe it was, called Timeline, which was for the 125th anniversary of the Conservatory. Do you recall that?
Of course. Yeah. Absolutely.
Tell us a little about that, how it was in your view.

It’s a multi-layered composition that I had the nerve to make it a three- hour-long composition involving music of all the times that the Conservatory was growing and the country was growing and getting in the essence of all and everything and emerging with a doable piece of music. It’s three hours long.
I understand it was for symphony orchestra, for jazz orchestra, klezmer, a soloist.
It was for all kinds of things, all of that.
Wow, that sounds really large, when you think of those different venues and see them in your mind.
It was the first time that all of the departments in the Conservatory had ever done anything together as a project.
Is that right?
And probably the last time.

And probably the last time. It was extraordinary. There were people who had never spoken to each other before, who had been at the Conservatory for decades, who were forced to have to work together. So it actually turned out to be an amazingly sort of harmonious experience for everybody involved. At one time we had the symphony, the chorus, the jazz orchestra, the klezmer, some assorted other instruments, Jimmy Giuffee, Bob Moses, and others on stage at one time. It was an extraordinary event. Some of the critics panned it, and some of them just loved it, because they got what we were doing, the past 125 years of musical history.
It sounds like it was a huge – but good time, a very good time. A couple years later, just using the years as a signpost for the ’90s, you did a re-orchestration of Living
Time that was commissioned by the Cité de la Musique and premiered by your orchestra with strings from the Paris Conservatoire Supérieur?

Um-hmm. It was a composition, Living Time, the composition, and had – I was lucky to have a French player who had a style – had Bill Evans’s style and could step in for Bill. He did a marvelous job. It’s an excellent piece, probably not important in America, but the French went for it.
America’s loss, really. America has overlooked so many things. I won’t comment beyond that, but . . .
No, go ahead.

It’s the age-old – I don’t want to call it a conundrum, but it’s the age-old situation that’s always existed, and that is that our artists are usually more fully appreciated by others, and in particular the Europeans. They know good music when they hear it. They know quality people when they see them. Both of those, I think, apply to you, Mr. Russell.
Grazie, grazie mille.

Around mid-decade we have you doing It’s About Time. The concept seemed to really be in terms of vertical form and Lydian and really just at a peak. Those are my words and my feelings. I’m very – that’s one of my favorites, It’s About Time.
That’s an honor, because you have a great sensibility and love for that kind of music.

It strikes me that that’s an incredible title, considering everything that was going on in the world at that time. Of course, I’m speaking from a somewhat American- centric point of view, because I live here, but I’m thinking about all that was going on in America at the time. The Congress had changed, and there was this whole business of the Contract with America, and the Republicans were still very much on the attack with respect to Bill Clinton. The economy was soaring. Socially, there were all kind of things going on in this country, because the O. J. Simpson trial was taking place. So there was a tremendous divide among people. Race had become an issue because of that, again. It was just a good year after Michael Jackson’s first big brush with the law. There were many, many other things going on across the country. So it was a turbulent period, and in the world as well. There were many things going on. The business with Iraq was very much happening, with the no-fly zone and the constant bombings. Africa was in great turmoil. We had just finished one of the worst holocaust, 800,000 people killed in Rwanda, which the world should still be – we should still be angry at ourselves about the
way we turned our backs on them. So there were all these things going on, and there are others I could mention, and you write this piece, It’s About Time. So so much can be read.
[said ironically:] And that helped a lot, right?
Yes.
That helped straighten things out.

One of the functions of an artist is to make people think, and to allow us to move to our own conclusions, our own thoughts about things. So when people see a great work like this being performed, they’ll come away with their own interpretation. That’s going to happen invariably. We’ve been talking about that in various contexts this evening. But I’m just struck by the title, and I’m hoping you’ll share with us some of your thoughts about why you titled it It’s About Time.
I’d reached a point in life when that title suited it. It was about time for various things to happen in the world and in regards to myself. That’s it. It’s about time. It fits a lot of situations.
It does. It truly does. Was that a commissioned piece?
Yeah. It was again Bosse Broberg commissioned the Swedish orchestra to play that piece. It was premiered in Stockholm.

It was a joint commission. The Arts Council of Great Britain was the other commissioner. So we premiered it in Stockholm and then took it to London to do it with the Living Time Orchestra. It was premiered, though, by the Swedish jazz orchestra. So it had two different performances for the premiere.

Alice, it strikes me, there have been many commissions for George’s work over the years. I can’t think of another artist – and I’m not talking about jazz artists now. I’m talking about in terms of music – who has gotten as many important commissions over the last 10 to 20 years as you have. And the interesting thing about it is, people don’t really know about the commissions, one, because there’s all this hype for the commercial side of the music. But am I correct that there really isn’t anyone else who’s gotten as many commissions as George has? Can you think of anyone, Alice?
I’m really not conversant with that world other than how it pertains to George. I’m sure there have been. I would assume Bobby Brookmeyer gets a lot of commissions.
He does get some, yeah.

He’s hooked up into that world. I think George isn’t really hooked up into that world in terms of going out and looking for things. But they have come to him, primarily, I think, because of him having lived in Europe and having developed a reputation there. But he is sought out. He hasn’t been doing any commissions, so that he could get the books done. So he stopped doing any real writing a few years ago. But I’m sure there’ll be other commissions in the future.
That’s true, isn’t it? The commissions haven’t really come from America.
Several have. But most of them are European.

It think what’s interesting, you’re not plugged in, you’re not actively seeking them, because you’ve been busy with very important things, your book, which has come out, and we’ve mentioned a few times, and we’re going to talk about almost exclusively here in a moment, but yet important commissions have come your way, from like the [?McKem] Fund for the Library of Congress, the one I mentioned earlier, the Cité de la Musique. I think it’s noteworthy when one considers that in the case of someone like Brookmeyer, for example, with all due respect to him, he’s plugged into that world. In 1997, just moving up a few years chronologically, you were elected as a foreign member to the Royal Swedish Academy of Music, a foreign member. I don’t know if people realize how significant that truly is. They’re not bringing in foreign members to their Academy of Music every day.

Duke Ellington is a foreign member. I think it’s Duke and Keith Jarrett, which is an odd choice in my opinion, but I think there are only three jazz – so-called jazz musicians, although I don’t consider Duke and George actually jazz musicians. They are musicians. But I think those are the only three in the so-called jazz milieu.
Stockhausen is a foreign member.
Stockhausen and Boulez. Yeah, but I’m talking about jazz specifically.
Who’s the others?
Boulez, Pierre Boulez.
Pierre Boulez, Karl-Heinz Stockhausen.
Stockhausen. It’s quite an impressive roster.

Well, it’s quite an honor. Let me congratulate you belatedly. I think it’s very important. Again, like the commissions, people don’t know about these things. At that point, you were working on a book? Had you gotten back to working on a book?
I must have been working on a book. That’s all I’ve been working on for 30 years. I mean, it’s not all I’ve been working on. I’ve been doing the commissions and stuff, but it’s the main thing.

If anyone has picked up on this oral history right at this point, let me say that the book we’re talking about is The Lydian Chromatic Concept of Tonal Organization, volume I: The Art and Science of Tonal Gravity. I want to read to you something that I found very interesting that Toru Takemitsu – I hope I’m pronouncing his name corrrectly – said. He said, “The Lydian Chromatic Concept is one of the two most splendid books about music.” I’m going to jump down here. “Though I’m considered a contemporary music composer, if I dared categorize myself as an artist, I’ve been strongly influenced by the Lydian concept, which is not simply a music method. We might call it a philosophy of music, or we might call it poetry.” I thought that was a beautiful and brilliant thing to say.
Blessings to – my man. What’s his name?
Takemitsu. Toru Takemitsu.

Yeah, Takemitsu. He has vision. He did practically singlehanded all of the movie music that came out of Japan, all of it. That’s no small job. So everything in the Japanese movies, it was Toru who not only did the music, but he did the sound. If a certain sound was needed, like an early morning sound and the people waking up, he directed that. He died much too young.
He actually translated George’s first book, the original Lydian Chromatic Concept, into Japanese for his own purposes. We found that out when we met him in Japan.
Is that right.
Yeah. So he had done that probably in the ’60s, and we met him 30 years later. He had actually requested the meeting with George when we went to Japan the first time. He became a good friend.

Someone who seems to agree with that, a gentleman that’s been associated with you for close to 50 years – he’s been a student of yours. He’s played in groups that you’ve led – David Baker said, “The foremost theoretical contribution of our time, destined to become the most influential philosophy of the future.” So he – philosophy, that word comes up again. I know we touched upon this yesterday. One of the things that we talked about was unity, in terms of a philosophical concept, and the unity that you want people to feel when they – and experience when they hear your music.

That’s right. It is a philosophy. What makes it a philosophy is its own science. It speaks to you. It actually is alive. It speaks to you. It’s self-made. That means that it – by itself, it has evolved to this, becoming the great singular scale that controls and sees all kinds of music, that embraces all kinds of music. You had – people – you had the major-scale philosophy. That didn’t do anything but create ii-V-I. It had its avoid notes. Very peculiar kind of a system. It was no system, actually. As I said, the Concept is self-made. It’s alive. It’s growing. Whereas the ordinary music had this, as I said, ii-V­ I, I being the major scale. What about when you – what do you do with the note that is not the fifth, but the augmented fifth, but still it’s a major with an augmented fifth? Well, you call it the augmented major scale. What about when there’s a – it’s a major chord, but it’s diminished major, with the flat third in it? You call it a Lydian diminished major. Lydian flat-seventh major, one of the great sounds of northern Ireland, music like that. That’s why the Irish can play the blues. Blues is not new to the Irish. So there are seven major chords that are major in every way. And it wouldn’t be possible without the Lydian augmented – I mean the Lydian chromatic concept.
The Lydian augmented, the Lydian diminished, the Lydian flat seventh.
Yeah, the Lydian chromatic.
The Lydian chromatic, of course, auxiliary augment.
It goes up to seven major chords.
You have in your book – a wonderful chart in the back of this book that lays all of that out, so that . . .
I sure do.

. . . an aspiring musician who wants to study this concept when he or she gets the book, this chart – it’s called chart A – is absolutely perfect for a way to approach and to continue to study and keep in mind the different laws that you talk about. Hold that for a second. I want to jump to something and then come back. May I do that? Or did you want to make a point? Because I didn’t want to cut you off.
I was going to make a point, because I can’t – I don’t have glasses.
Please do. Okay. Did you need this?
All of these have major chords.
Right, Lydian major thirteenth.
Yeah. Start here.
I don’t think we want to read them. We don’t need to read all of them, because that wouldn’t make much sense to someone just listening to this.
But anyone getting the book, the thing that will really resonate for them is that they can look at each of the Lydian scales and then see all the chord-scale unity that relates.
That’s right.

That’s critically important, because a musician has to often change his or her way of thinking in order to really approach this properly. They’ve got to kind of, as the French say, coup de torchon, wipe the slate clean and approach this in a virginal sense. Here’s something I found particularly fascinating, George. I was reading through your book last night. I ran across the street last night, and I xeroxed this, so I’d actually have it in my hand and wouldn’t have to thumb through the book. On page 52 you talk about the principle of tonal gravity. I hope you’ll just touch upon this again. People can actually do their own lessons when they get the book, which I recommend that everybody do. But you start off, you say, “The one phenomenon that can be categorized as a higher law of The Lydian Chromatic Concept of Tonal Organization is tonal gravity.” I want to jump down a little bit, because you alluded to this earlier. “As an objective-oriented principle, tonal gravity, in this manner, frees music from the subjective notions of right and wrong tones – clearing a path for the reunification of music with physics.”
It is the science.

That whole business of, when you’re dealing with the major and the minor scale, you can easily get into a wrong note, wrong tone, whereas – and it’s not going to happen overnight, but if one studies and applies oneself to the Concept, I think they’ll come to understand the real gravity, if you will, of that phrase.

You guys – and this is addressed to both of you, because Alice, you’ve been very involved in some of the organization and the many things that are attendant to making a heavy project like a book work, and in addition to any book being a heavy project, when you have a heavy book, in terms of subject matter, all of that is just exponentially increased. What are some of the things that you’d like to say about this book, just in general terms? I’ve been talking about it, but I think people would be interested in, and Alice, you’ve been very close to it. You’re not a musician, are you?
I play, but I’m not a professional musician. No.

But certainly – let me just interject my own little editorial comment here. You seem like a musician in terms of your sensitivity and your knowledge about the music on a number of different levels. It is very impressive. That’s why I thought I better ask. I’ve never seen you pick up an instrument. But I happen to personally believe one doesn’t necessarily have to know how to play to be a musician.
I agree.
A subject for another discussion, but . . .
I think you’re – I agree with that.

But I’m curious. I’d like for you to address this first, and then you, George, but as a person who’s been close to the project for a long time now. Just freestyle a little bit, if you would, about this book and what you think it might mean to people.

For me, it’s the culmination of a life’s work that I’ve been privileged to be a part of in some small way for almost three decades. It represents an enormous amount of sacrifice on George’s part. I’ve never seen a human being so determined to do something and to do it thoroughly and right. It was nights and days of endless work with him sitting in that little studio working non-stop. When you say he’s working on a book, people think, oh, maybe an hour or two a night in his spare time. This was literally 18-, 19-hour days, when he wasn’t teaching, when we weren’t touring, any other time – and when he wasn’t getting some exercise that he needs to stay afloat – he was working on the book. So it has been an enormous burden and task for both of us. At some point, I never thought I would see the book be a reality. I felt it was going to be impossible to finally get it into shape to publish it. But things happened, and they moved very quickly when we did finally get it into shape, and now we have what I think is a beautiful book that is going to be the music theory for the 21st-century.
It is a good looking book, too. I have to say . . .
Thank you. It costs us enough.
. . . I really like the way it looks.
It’s a good looking woman who got it together.
We agree
We also had a beautiful editor, a guy, Scott Kuzowski, who edited the book – who’s also a musician – who did the layout and did everything, I think, remarkably well.
The cover means that it was like climbing this mountain. This is a mountain out in . . .
Utah, a Minor White photograph. It’s Utah, I believe.
In Utah? Yeah. It – who’s the . . .
Miner White, a man that you knew, the photographer.

Miner White, the great, great Miner White, took this picture. Scott and his wife did the cover. It’s meant to be a – like climbing this peak to working on The Concept. I wouldn’t be able to do it unless The Concept was feeding me. I mean, it feed me and directed me. It’s alive. That means that gravity’s alive. That’s what it turns out to be. A fellow that works with me, we both came to the conclusion, that we’re into – we’re in the skies now, because there are things connected here to the science of – what do you call it?
Tonal gravity?
No, no.
Physics?
Physics, yeah. And I didn’t graduate from high school.

But you’ve certainly graduated from the university of cosmicology. Up to this point we’ve been talking about the ’90s, and we’ve fast-forwarded a bit to 2001 and, right now, 2004, which brings us current with the book. I want to mention
something that I think it important that it not be overlooked, in the late ’90s, 1999, I had the . . .
Can I interrupt?
Please do.
Why don’t we go and have dinner?
There won’t be editing, right? That’ll make anyone listening hungry. Soon, I hope.
It will make them see that you have a – you’ve heavy, but you have a sense of humor.
Think he’s always driven by food.
He’s driven by practical considerations.
Where do the food be?
Where da food?
Where my food at?
Where the money?
Anyhow, Bob was saying.

I was saying that I had the pleasure of meeting you, after talking to you on the phone for several years, at Tribeca, Manhattan Borough College, down in lower Manhattan, where you – where we did a live interview, first of all, in front of a couple hundred people, which was wonderful and very enlightening and stimulating for me. In addition to that, it was a historic concert that your International Living Time Orchestra performed later that evening. It was the first time that you had appeared in New York in 20 years. There was a tremendous level of excitement. I know, because I was there. I talked to people. There were – there may have been hundreds. I know for a fact that there were dozens, because I saw about 20 to 30 that I personally knew.
Was that the Living Time Orchestra?
Yes.
From London and all?

Yes, and there were dozens of musicians who not only came to the interview, because they were anxious to hear you talk about your Concept, which you did, and you demonstrated on a piano. It was absolutely superb. I loved it. And then the concert, which was fantastic, two nights later. Again, courtesy, or as part of the [?McKem] Fund commission for the Library of Congress, you performed at the Library of Congress auditorium, one of their music halls – Coolidge, I believe it is – in a sold-out, packed concert that was tremendously well received. Again you had your International Living Time Orchestra. Fantastic.
Yeah. This was the music of the people.

We danced. We were moving out there in the audience. The great thing about that hall, there’s not a bad sightline anywhere. I have said any number of times over the course of these four tapes, the International Living Time Orchestra – your musicians are from all over, aren’t they?
They’re mostly from London.
And the States. It’s half and half. It’s American, half British, with the occasional melancholy Dane, who’s Palle Mikkelborg on trumpet.
Tiger Okoshi, a Japanese gentleman
Yep, but from Boston, Tiger.
Japanese-American.
Right. Andy Shepherd, the wonderful saxophonist from London

In the 21st-century, we’ve seen a completion of the book, again, The Lydian Chromatic Concept of Tonal Organization, volume I: The Art and Science of Tonal Gravity. That says to me that there’s a volume II in our future.
There is.
Tell us. Talk to us.
Sometimes I feel like a – I was going to say, almost said, sometimes I feel like a motherless child, because I used that song in the school program that was three . . .
Time Line?
Time Line. I used . . .
Oh, okay. For the Conservatory
I used – sometimes I used Sometimes I Feel Like a Motherless Child. It was very touching. But I lost what I should have been . . .
If I talk, I’m sure you’ll think of it, and then I want you to interrupt me.
Put me back on track.
Volume II.
I see that it says volume I: The Art and Science. Is there a volume II in our future?

Oh yes. There is a volume II. It’s the heart and soul – it puts all of this together and makes it possible to deal with it much easier and see the logic of it. As I said, there are hints that it’s getting into physics and the stars.
It is beautiful. You say in your epilogue in the book, which begins on page 235, “The major scale and the Lydian scale represent opposing forces in nature.”
[recording interrupted]

George, one thing I’d like to do, we’ve been talking about this book for several hours now, The Lydian Chromatic Concept of Tonal Organization, volume I: The Art and Science of Tonal Gravity. I would like to read a couple of things from the epilogue for anyone listening to this tape in the future, because I think it not only continues to underscore the Concept as we’ve talked about it – and we’ve talked about it politically, economically, socially. We’ve talked about it musically and in very – at times spoken of it in very technical musical terms – but I must stress that for anyone who is interested, they should get the book. I want to mention your website one more time. It’s the lydianchromaticconcept.com and georgerussell.com. People can go to that as well and learn about you, about your music, find out how to get the book, volume I. In your epilogue, you say, “The major scale and the Lydian scale represent opposing forces in

nature, the active horizontal resolving force and the passive vertical unity force, respectively. It’s not a matter of which is best, for both forces are present and functioning in all of nature.” I’m going to skip down a bit. In a couple of paragraphs below that, you say, “When human consciousness allows itself to become blind to the second and third passive and neutralizing forces, the unrestrained active force alone rules life, and the Darwinian aspects of that condition become more and more apparent.” Both of those speak to what has always been and what is very much prevalent now. In closing on my part – and I would like for you to say – make any comment or say anything that you wish to, you and/or Alice, this book salutes, as a true renaissance, the extraordinary era between the turn of the century through the mid-1980s, amidst all of its violence, psychological as well as physical, artistic innovation and recognition of levels of experience will continue to survive as the enabling factors in the evolution of all the arts. The Lydian Chromatic Concept is proud to be a creation of that fantastic era. In closing, I must say that, when I questioned the why of the more than 50 years spent in developing the Concepy, the most gratifying and sustaining thought lies in knowing that the highest aim of the Concept is to shed light on the way in which cosmic gravity manifests in the realm of musical sound, to leave no doubt that gravity, magnetism, is a conscious, living objective force. I hope this knowledge will light your way, inspiring and empowering your essence to express its truest, most unique self, not only musically, but also daring to venture into music’s womb, that unseen, philo-spiritual world which is music’s seminal source and a foundation connecting it and you to the stars. George Russell, Jamaica Plain, Massachusetts, June 6, 2000. Thank you, George and Alice.
It’s a pleasure, Bob. Thank you.

You closed with grace, and you opened with grace, and you’ve been graceful all the way through. We’re going to have to take a long time to come to the realization that there are words that we’ve spoken that evidently, if nature decides, can be heard a hundred years, two hundred years from now. That’s a very high honor. Both Alice and I thank you and thank the powers that be. Give them my best. As I say, in a minute, as Don Cherry would say. Just to close, with Don Cherry, you know he was in Stockholm for a long time. His sister became famous, because she sang with a very popular group, rock group. So when Don found out that he was probably not going to survive very long, he moved in with his sister, who had a nice home somewhere. I don’t know if it was northern Italy or what.
It’s his daughter.

On the day that he felt that he was going to leave us, he went upstairs, dressed in his dressy suit, tie and everything, and came back down, grabbed her hand and left. That was it. He left in style. I like style. I wish I had more of it. Yeah, this is a heavy, heavy thing, man.
Now what do you want to do for dinner?
(transcribed and edited by Barry Kernfeld)

segments.chapter: Cincinnati childhood and adoption
segments.title: Opening of the interview, Jamaica Plain
segments.summary: Daughtry introduces the session at Russell's home and confirms his birth in Cincinnati in 1923.

segments.chapter: Cincinnati childhood and adoption
segments.title: Early Cincinnati, boarding with musicians, neighbor Jimmy Mundy
segments.summary: Russell recalls kindergarten, his nurse mother boarding him with families who hosted riverboat musicians, and neighbor Jimmy Mundy, who persuaded his mother to let him be a musician.

segments.chapter: Cincinnati childhood and adoption
segments.title: Singing with Fats Waller and hearing Art Tatum practice
segments.summary: Russell recalls disliking school, singing as a Boy Scout with Fats Waller at the YMCA, and hearing Tatum practice in rooming houses; Daughtry notes the network of homes that hosted musicians.

segments.chapter: Cincinnati childhood and adoption
segments.title: Expelled from high school, first drums and the Wilberforce scholarship
segments.summary: He rebelled against school, was expelled over his clothes, took Hemingway's advice to live life, and won a drum scholarship to Wilberforce; his mother had bought a used drum set.

segments.chapter: Cincinnati childhood and adoption
segments.title: Extended family in St. Louis and childhood nicknames
segments.summary: Asked about family, he describes the St. Louis relatives, Aunt Nannie's biscuits, and nicknames such as Long George Kelly and George Allen.

segments.chapter: Cincinnati childhood and adoption
segments.title: Father Uncle Joe, the railroad chef, and trips on the train
segments.summary: His adoptive father, a railroad chef who loved horses and cards, took him on trips where he sold ice cream; Daughtry comments on the railroad in black culture.

segments.chapter: Cincinnati childhood and adoption
segments.title: Learning he was adopted from Army papers
segments.summary: He describes his parents' unhappy marriage, finding out about the adoption from Army papers in World War II, and Daughtry's reflections on adoption then and now.

segments.chapter: Cincinnati childhood and adoption
segments.title: His biological parents: a wealthy Kentucky mother and an Oberlin professor
segments.summary: He never met his biological parents; he learned his mother came from a wealthy family and his white father was a music professor at Oberlin.

segments.chapter: Cincinnati childhood and adoption
segments.title: Principal reveals his biological father asked about him
segments.summary: On being expelled he learns from the principal that his father had inquired about him, accepts his situation, and heads to Wilberforce on a scholarship at about 17.

segments.chapter: Cincinnati childhood and adoption
segments.title: Mother's St. Louis people and father's Georgia roots
segments.summary: He explains the St. Louis family, his mother's origin, and visits to his father's home near Marietta, Georgia, where he felt uncomfortable.

segments.chapter: Wilberforce and the South
segments.title: Segregated train to the South with his mother
segments.summary: He recalls being forced to move to the back of the train in Tennessee, his stern nurse mother, and her stoic reaction.

segments.chapter: Wilberforce and the South
segments.title: Touring the South with the Wilberforce Singers
segments.summary: As drummer with the Wilberforce Singers he sang in swamp churches and met a preacher who milked rattlesnakes; they discuss Wilberforce's church and state character.

segments.chapter: Wilberforce and the South
segments.title: Getting to Wilberforce, losing his money, the Wilberforce band
segments.summary: He lost his savings gambling the night before leaving, got the money back, spent a semester at Wilberforce, and was recalled when the replacement drummer was bad.

segments.chapter: Wilberforce and the South
segments.title: Riverboat bands and Fate Marable in Cincinnati
segments.summary: Daughtry asks about river bands; Russell recalls riverboat drummers staying at his house, one romancing his cousin, and bands moving from New Orleans to St. Louis to Cincinnati.

segments.chapter: Benny Carter and Cincinnati
segments.title: Adolescence and early lessons from women in Chicago
segments.summary: Asked about girls, he credits women, especially a young runaway dancer in Chicago, with teaching him about life.

segments.chapter: Benny Carter and Cincinnati
segments.title: Drumming with Benny Carter until Max Roach replaced him
segments.summary: Carter hired him in Cincinnati during the war; he describes the band, lateness with J. J. Johnson in Chicago, and being replaced by Max Roach.

segments.chapter: Benny Carter and Cincinnati
segments.title: Fitz, the white bassist beaten by detectives in Cincinnati
segments.summary: In Spaulding Givens's trio a white bassist was beaten by two white detectives for playing with black musicians; officials did nothing and Russell grew to hate Cincinnati.

segments.chapter: Benny Carter and Cincinnati
segments.title: Spaulding Givens, later Nadi Qamar
segments.summary: A digression on where Spaulding Givens went and that he is still living as Nadi Qamar.

segments.chapter: Benny Carter and Cincinnati
segments.title: Gangsters and corrupt police around the music; being cased in Chicago
segments.summary: Daughtry raises the gangster and police element in jazz; Russell recalls being stopped by men in cars and claiming Spanish and Irish nationality.

segments.chapter: Benny Carter and Cincinnati
segments.title: Chain gang gunfire and a car wreck on the Singers' Southern trip
segments.summary: Driving with the Wilberforce Singers in Georgia, they ran a chain-gang sign and were shot at; in Maryland they saw a wreck. He swore never to return, and describes the Singers' repertoire.

segments.chapter: Tuberculosis and learning to write
segments.title: Time at Wilberforce and being drafted
segments.summary: He explains his time at Wilberforce, clarifies he was drafted rather than enlisting, and recalls his romantic wish to be a Marine.

segments.chapter: Tuberculosis and learning to write
segments.title: Harold Gaston, Jimmy Blanton and tuberculosis
segments.summary: He credits tuberculosis with giving him six months in a hospital room, and recalls Harold Gaston, who taught him to write and died of TB soon after Blanton.

segments.chapter: Tuberculosis and learning to write
segments.title: Learning to write music in the Branch sanitarium
segments.summary: Gaston got him started writing; he composed his first piece without a piano and realized he was a writer, not a drummer, planting the germ of the Lydian Concept.

segments.chapter: Tuberculosis and learning to write
segments.title: Discharged from the hospital after a protest and an incident with a nurse
segments.summary: He and Gaston were discharged after protesting segregation in the lunch hall and after he was caught with a nurse.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Dizzy Gillespie
segments.title: Destitute in Chicago and Foster Johnson's studio
segments.summary: After leaving the hospital he slept in the streets until a dancer, Foster Johnson, gave him studio space.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Dizzy Gillespie
segments.title: Writing the nightclub opening for Earl Hines
segments.summary: He stayed up four nights writing the opening for Earl Hines at a gangster-owned club; a wrong key signature was fixed, the review was good, and he scraped by at a drugstore.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Dizzy Gillespie
segments.title: Little Diz and Little Bird, the bus to New York and the Hotel Theresa
segments.summary: He recalls two Chicago kids nicknamed Little Diz and Little Bird, then three of them arriving in New York with $5 and staying at the Hotel Theresa.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Dizzy Gillespie
segments.title: Skippy Williams and Ellington's band in Cincinnati; selling one piece to the bands
segments.summary: He hosted Ellington sidemen in Cincinnati, later lived with Skippy Williams in New York, and lived on one piece he sold to many bands.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Dizzy Gillespie
segments.title: New World and the introduction for Dizzy Gillespie
segments.summary: The piece New World began in the sanitarium; Dizzy heard it and Russell wrote an introduction and ending for his Carnegie Hall concert.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Dizzy Gillespie
segments.title: Carnegie Hall and Boston with Chano Pozo
segments.summary: He recalls suggesting Chano Pozo's jungle outfit and chant, the next night at Boston's Symphony Hall, and the difficulty communicating with Chano.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Dizzy Gillespie
segments.title: Losing the Cubana Be score in a taxi
segments.summary: He left the score of Cubana Be, Cubana Bop in a taxi, and Gil Fuller rebuilt it from the recording.

segments.chapter: Hospital, Miles Davis and Gil Evans
segments.title: Dating his second, longer hospital stay
segments.summary: They try to date the 15-month second hospitalization, placing it c. 1945-46, between Benny Carter and Dizzy.

segments.chapter: Hospital, Miles Davis and Gil Evans
segments.title: Daughtry on researching the interview and Miles's birthday
segments.summary: After a recording break, Daughtry explains his preparation, the repeated TB error, and a story about Miles's birthday and Fred Foss's son.

segments.chapter: Hospital, Miles Davis and Gil Evans
segments.title: Tape two: the 1940s and a guiding spirit
segments.summary: Daughtry resumes on tape two; Russell says he follows impulses and trusts forces that guided him through hardship.

segments.chapter: Hospital, Miles Davis and Gil Evans
segments.title: In the hospital showing Miles Davis how modes work
segments.summary: Near death, Russell remembers Miles wanting to learn all the changes; later he showed Miles modes on the piano, and Miles began playing modally.

segments.chapter: Hospital, Miles Davis and Gil Evans
segments.title: Healing, positive thinking and Dr. Weil's book
segments.summary: Russell says music kept him from dwelling on illness and recommends a book by Andrew Weil.

segments.chapter: Hospital, Miles Davis and Gil Evans
segments.title: Arranging for Ventura, Shaw and Thornhill; Gil Evans's gift for color
segments.summary: Asked about arranging for Charlie Ventura, Artie Shaw and Claude Thornhill, Russell contrasts his melodic focus with Gil Evans's orchestral color.

segments.chapter: Hospital, Miles Davis and Gil Evans
segments.title: Gil Evans's basement apartment and the Apollo arranging job
segments.summary: He describes Gil's one-room apartment as a sanctuary for Mulligan, Bird and Miles, Gil's 'drive a taxi' advice, and an all-night job for a band at the Apollo.

segments.chapter: Hospital, Miles Davis and Gil Evans
segments.title: Sylvia Goldberg, the pianist at Gil's place
segments.summary: He recalls pianist Sylvia Goldberg, who played Bach and Bud Powell and was beloved by the circle, and Bird sleeping at the apartment.

segments.chapter: Hospital, Miles Davis and Gil Evans
segments.title: Juilliard visits and living on Park Avenue after John Lewis rescued him
segments.summary: He recalls going to Juilliard rehearsals with Gil, Miles and Mulligan, a Park Avenue patron, and John Lewis pulling him out of the Bowery.

segments.chapter: Hospital, Miles Davis and Gil Evans
segments.title: Elvin Jones's illness and a recording break
segments.summary: Brief talk about Elvin Jones being gravely ill before a break.

segments.chapter: Lydian book publication and marriage to Juanita
segments.title: Tape 2 continued, May 5th
segments.summary: Daughtry reopens the session on May 5, 2004.

segments.chapter: Lydian book publication and marriage to Juanita
segments.title: A Bird in Igor's Yard and Benny Goodman
segments.summary: Daughtry asks about A Bird in Igor's Yard; Russell recalls Goodman rejecting it, the DeFranco recording, and a Dutch fan whose letters finally got it released 20 years later.

segments.chapter: Lydian book publication and marriage to Juanita
segments.title: Buckwheat, Dave Guard and the Kingston Trio discover the Concept
segments.summary: Asked how the Lydian book was published, Russell explains that Kingston Trio bassist Buckwheat and founder Dave Guard became fascinated with the Concept.

segments.chapter: Lydian book publication and marriage to Juanita
segments.title: Dave Guard's $5,000 check and what happened to Guard and Buckwheat
segments.summary: Guard sent a $5,000 check that paid for publication; Russell describes Guard's death in Australia and Buckwheat's mutilation.

segments.chapter: Lydian book publication and marriage to Juanita
segments.title: Worries about repeating stories, and the book's first publication in 1953
segments.summary: Russell asks whether his stories could bother relatives; Daughtry recaps the check and the 1953 publication.

segments.chapter: Lydian book publication and marriage to Juanita
segments.title: Juanita Odjenar, his first wife
segments.summary: He credits Juanita, later married to Jimmy Giuffre, for support, and explains the tune Odjenar.

segments.chapter: Lydian book publication and marriage to Juanita
segments.title: Meeting Juanita through Dizzy at John Lewis's house
segments.summary: He tells how Dizzy walked Juanita into the bathroom where he sat covered in Magic Shave while living with John Lewis in Jamaica.

segments.chapter: Lydian book publication and marriage to Juanita
segments.title: Marriage with Juanita and working on the Concept
segments.summary: They married within months, lived in a hotel by her office, and she supported him while he worked on the Concept.

segments.chapter: Lydian book publication and marriage to Juanita
segments.title: Juanita copying music for Mingus and Gil
segments.summary: He taught Juanita to copy music; her errors on Mingus's and Gil's pieces forced him to stay up fixing them.

segments.chapter: Lydian book publication and marriage to Juanita
segments.title: Marriage ending after the Lenox seminar
segments.summary: The marriage began to break up around the Lenox School of Jazz when Juanita met Jimmy Giuffre.

segments.chapter: Lenox, RCA and Bill Evans
segments.title: Teaching Concept at the Lenox School of Jazz
segments.summary: John Lewis arranged the school; Russell taught the Concept to students including Ornette Coleman, Don Cherry and the Heaths.

segments.chapter: Lenox, RCA and Bill Evans
segments.title: Ornette Coleman's impact and the river trip analogy
segments.summary: Russell says Ornette opened the door to 'supra-vertical' tonal gravity; Daughtry recalls the river-trip analogy and Ornette's praise of the Concept.

segments.chapter: Lenox, RCA and Bill Evans
segments.title: What the Lydian Chromatic Concept covers
segments.summary: He explains the Lydian chromatic scale as containing all scales, claims it explains music beyond Bach where 400 years of theory failed, and Daughtry laments school teaching.

segments.chapter: Lenox, RCA and Bill Evans
segments.title: Teaching Ornette and equal temperament
segments.summary: Russell calls the Lenox students a gift, says Ornette showed him how to include everything, and says he only deals with equal temperament.

segments.chapter: Lenox, RCA and Bill Evans
segments.title: Jack Lewis at RCA Victor and the Jazz Workshop
segments.summary: He explains how RCA's jazz director Jack Lewis recorded his group with Hal McKusick, Bill Evans and Art Farmer, gave him money to leave the Bowery, and was later fired.

segments.chapter: Lenox, RCA and Bill Evans
segments.title: Meeting Bill Evans on the Staten Island ferry
segments.summary: In the Bowery years he took a singer's quiet companion on a ferry ride and discovered he was pianist Bill Evans.

segments.chapter: Lenox, RCA and Bill Evans
segments.title: Moving to the Village; Juanita, Jimmy Giuffre and Parkinson's
segments.summary: Russell recounts moving to the Village with Jack's money, Juanita's affair with Jimmy Giuffre, and visiting them each Christmas.

segments.chapter: Lenox, RCA and Bill Evans

segments.summary: He drove Bill Evans and Barry Galbraith to a Bed-Stuy club where Miles gave Bill Red Garland's chair at intermission, leading to Kind of Blue.

segments.summary: Daughtry lists the great recordings of the period including Jazz in the Space Age and Ezz-thetics; Russell says he does not look back.

segments.chapter: Leaving for Scandinavia

segments.summary: Russell says he wants his music to have depth and meaning, then criticizes Time-Life's televised spiritual shows.

segments.title: Listen to the Silence and its premiere in Norway
segments.summary: He explains Listen to the Silence, premiered in the oldest church in Norway as a response to cruelty and war, and its neglect by the New England Conservatory.

segments.chapter: Leaving for Scandinavia
segments.title: Tape 3 opening, May 5th
segments.summary: Daughtry opens tape three.

segments.chapter: Leaving for Scandinavia
segments.title: Why he left America for Europe in the 1960s
segments.summary: Russell says the free-music scene without structure and Cold War politics drove him away.

segments.chapter: Leaving for Scandinavia
segments.title: Choosing Sweden, ill after a botched operation, and the George Wein tour
segments.summary: He chose neutral Sweden, left a George Wein world tour in poor health after a botched operation, and arranged a club date in Stockholm.

segments.chapter: Leaving for Scandinavia
segments.title: Bosse Broberg and Swedish Radio

segments.title: The Norwegian mountain ledge that inspired Trip to Pillarguri
segments.summary: In Norway a host led him sideways along a ledge above an 1800-foot drop; Russell turned back and later wrote a tune about it.

segments.chapter: Leaving for Scandinavia
segments.title: Writing Trip to Pillarguri and its meaning
segments.summary: He says he sets an emotional agenda before writing and that the piece is edgy, about surrendering back to good sense.

segments.chapter: Leaving for Scandinavia
segments.title: Marit Jerstad and Gurdjieff in Norway
segments.summary: He describes Marit, who introduced him to Gurdjieff, founded the Gurdjieff Foundation in Oslo, and helped get his music on Norwegian television.

segments.title: Guest conducting European radio orchestras and feeling valued
segments.summary: Daughtry marvels that an unknown American conducted radio orchestras across Scandinavia and Europe; Russell says it was the first time he felt accounted for.

segments.chapter: Leaving for Scandinavia

segments.summary: He heard Jan Garbarek and Terje Rypdal at a Norwegian festival, formed a group with them, and lost them to Manfred Eicher's ECM.

segments.summary: Russell and Daughtry discuss Garbarek crediting him as his first teacher and Rypdal's rock career.

segments.summary: Russell explains the German student Goetz Tangerding and his mother Charlotte, who helped start his band, and their deaths.

segments.chapter: European recordings and return to America
segments.title: Electronic Sonata and Othello: the albums and their labels
segments.summary: Russell describes Electronic Sonata made in Swedish Radio's electronic studio and the Norwegian Radio Othello ballet, while Daughtry sorts out the Flying Dutchman and Strata-East labels.

segments.chapter: European recordings and return to America
segments.title: The Othello ballet's choreographer and taking music somewhere new
segments.summary: They discuss integrating electronics, the Norwegian television production of Othello, and Russell's wish to take music to a place it has never been.

segments.chapter: European recordings and return to America
segments.title: Returning to America to teach at New England Conservatory
segments.summary: Gunther Schuller, then president, invited him to the Conservatory in 1969; Russell was no longer married.

segments.chapter: European recordings and return to America
segments.title: Conducting with Stockhausen for Danish radio
segments.summary: His sextet played at the Tivoli between two orchestras performing Stockhausen, and he became friends with the composer.

segments.chapter: European recordings and return to America
segments.title: Why he came home: Vietnam, protest and the music of the early 1970s
segments.summary: He missed America's grit; anti-American feeling over Vietnam in Scandinavia pushed him home, and Daughtry surveys the losses and rise of Motown and Strata-East.

segments.chapter: European recordings and return to America
segments.title: Listen to the Silence, Vietnam, Iraq and What's Going On
segments.summary: Asked if Listen to the Silence reflected Vietnam, Russell turns to Iraq, offers his view on Bush and Saddam, and praises What's Going On.

segments.chapter: European recordings and return to America
segments.title: Teaching the Concept once a week
segments.summary: He says he taught once weekly at the Conservatory and the Concept grew clearer.

segments.chapter: Teaching the Concept: gravity and the Lydian scale
segments.title: Vertical Form, Coltrane and Coleman Hawkins as vertical players
segments.summary: He explains that the Concept first named vertical and horizontal playing, contrasting Coltrane and Hawkins with Lester Young.

segments.chapter: Teaching the Concept: gravity and the Lydian scale
segments.title: Music as a science: a sarcastic Swedish host
segments.summary: A Swedish official joked about showing his book to the minister of science; Russell argues music is science because it is gravity.

segments.chapter: Teaching the Concept: gravity and the Lydian scale
segments.title: Discovering the Lydian scale in the tuberculosis hospital
segments.summary: He recalls playing the major and Lydian scales for months in the TB hospital's solarium and library, realizing the major scale is going somewhere while the Lydian scale is a unity.

segments.chapter: Teaching the Concept: gravity and the Lydian scale
segments.title: Gravity, the overtone series and why theory chose the major scale
segments.summary: He explains tonal gravity and the 11th overtone, claims Western theory chose the diatonic scale for marches, and says he found the science missing for 400 years.

segments.chapter: Teaching the Concept: gravity and the Lydian scale
segments.title: Hearing the scales on Alice's computer
segments.summary: Alice plays a computer demonstration of the difference between scales, and Daughtry names the Lydian Chromatic Concept websites.

segments.chapter: Later years: recordings, Alice and the book
segments.title: His son Jock
segments.summary: Russell describes his son Jock, born in Sweden in 1965, a traveler and filmmaker living in Stockholm.

segments.chapter: Later years: recordings, Alice and the book
segments.title: 1970s recordings: Living Time, Vertical Form VI and Live at the Vanguard
segments.summary: Daughtry reviews the 1970s recordings, including Living Time with Bill Evans and the Vanguard album with Sabu Martinez, and Russell says they still open shows with Living Time's theme.

segments.chapter: Later years: recordings, Alice and the book
segments.title: American labels, ECM and Giovanni Bonandrini
segments.summary: Pressed about record deals, Russell has nothing good to say about American labels or ECM, but credits Bonandrini with saving jazz recordings.

segments.chapter: Later years: recordings, Alice and the book
segments.title: Jazz is not sought; keeping quality high and danceable
segments.summary: Russell says jazz is last on the public's list, that his music is danceable, and that he wants listeners to feel they have traveled somewhere new.

segments.chapter: Later years: recordings, Alice and the book
segments.title: The African Game and the Grammy
segments.summary: Russell describes the Boston-assembled band behind The African Game, held back by Bruce Lundvall, which he thinks deserved a Grammy.

segments.chapter: Later years: recordings, Alice and the book
segments.title: 1980s recordings and the International Living Time Orchestra
segments.summary: Daughtry lists 1980s albums, Russell says he does not look back, and he describes touring with British and American players for the British Council.

segments.chapter: Later years: recordings, Alice and the book
segments.title: Tape 4 opening with Alice Russell
segments.summary: Daughtry opens tape four and Alice Russell joins.

segments.chapter: Later years: recordings, Alice and the book
segments.title: How George and Alice met
segments.summary: Alice recalls meeting George in St. Louis in 1976 when he came to recruit for the Conservatory; they have been married 27 years.

segments.chapter: Later years: recordings, Alice and the book
segments.title: Timeline for the Conservatory's 125th anniversary
segments.summary: Russell describes Timeline, a three-hour work for orchestra, jazz orchestra, klezmer and soloists; Alice says all departments worked together for the first time.

segments.chapter: Later years: recordings, Alice and the book
segments.title: Re-orchestrating Living Time for Paris
segments.summary: He tells of the Cite de la Musique commission with Paris Conservatoire strings and a French pianist in Bill Evans's style; Daughtry laments America's neglect.

segments.chapter: Later years: recordings, Alice and the book
segments.title: It's About Time, its title and commissions
segments.summary: Russell explains the title It's About Time, commissioned by Bosse Broberg and the Arts Council of Great Britain and premiered in Stockholm.

segments.chapter: Later years: recordings, Alice and the book
segments.title: Commissions and the Royal Swedish Academy of Music
segments.summary: Daughtry and Alice discuss the many European commissions, Russell not seeking them, and his 1997 election to the Royal Swedish Academy of Music.

segments.chapter: Later years: recordings, Alice and the book
segments.title: Toru Takemitsu's praise for the Concept
segments.summary: Daughtry reads Takemitsu's tribute to the Concept; Russell and Alice recall Takemitsu translating the first book into Japanese.

segments.chapter: Later years: recordings, Alice and the book
segments.title: The Concept as a philosophy and the seven major chords
segments.summary: After David Baker's praise, Russell says the Concept is self-made and alive and yields seven major chords, from augmented to Lydian flat-seventh.

segments.chapter: Later years: recordings, Alice and the book
segments.title: Chart A and the principle of tonal gravity
segments.summary: They discuss the book's chart of Lydian scales and the passage on tonal gravity freeing music from right-and-wrong notes.

segments.chapter: Later years: recordings, Alice and the book
segments.title: Alice on the book as a life's work, and its production
segments.summary: Alice describes George's 18-hour days on the book over three decades and its editor and design.

segments.chapter: Later years: recordings, Alice and the book
segments.title: The book's cover and the Concept as a living force
segments.summary: Russell explains the Minor White cover as climbing a mountain, says the Concept fed him, and that gravity is alive.

segments.chapter: Later years: recordings, Alice and the book
segments.title: Break for dinner
segments.summary: Russell interrupts to ask about dinner.

segments.chapter: Later years: recordings, Alice and the book
segments.title: The 1999 Tribeca interview and Living Time Orchestra concerts
segments.summary: Daughtry recalls the live interview in Manhattan, the first New York concert in 20 years, and the Library of Congress concert; Alice names band members.

segments.chapter: Later years: recordings, Alice and the book
segments.title: Volume II of the Concept
segments.summary: Russell says Volume II will tie the Concept together and head toward physics and the stars.

segments.chapter: Later years: recordings, Alice and the book
segments.title: Epilogue of the book read aloud
segments.summary: Daughtry reads from the epilogue about opposing forces and cosmic gravity, closing with the book's website.

segments.chapter: Later years: recordings, Alice and the book
segments.title: Closing thanks and Don Cherry's last day
segments.summary: Russell thanks Daughtry and tells how Don Cherry dressed up and left with his daughter on the day he died.
